paper_title: Reducing Representational Interference in Retrieval Embeddings with Trainable Prefix Tokens

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embedding models compress variable-length text into fixed-size vector representations, but this compression can entangle semantic content with residual token-level information, such as artifacts arising from attention sink behavior. We propose a simple method that prepends trainable [DUMP] tokens to the input during embedding model training. The method keeps the model architecture, pooling strategy, and training loss unchanged, while optimizing the added tokens through the standard contrastive retrieval objective. By introducing trainable prefix positions that interact with regular tokens during encoding, [DUMP] tokens help reduce the influence of residual or uninformative token-level signals on the final retrieval representation. Experiments on standard retrieval and long-context benchmarks show that our method consistently improves over finetuned baselines across encoder and decoder embedding models. Further analysis shows that [DUMP] tokens alter token-level activation and attention patterns associated with low-information tokens. These results suggest that trainable prefix tokens provide a lightweight way to improve retrieval representations.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Embedding models have become a fundamental component of mod-
ern retrieval systems, where queries and passages are mapped into
a shared vector space for efficient semantic matching [12, 19]. Their
effectiveness heavily depends on the ability to compress variable-
length text into fixed-dimensional representations while preserving
the critical semantic information relevant to retrieval across diverse
domains. This compression is typically performed through pooling
or token-selection strategies [14, 21], effectively forcing the model
to funnel rich contextual dynamics into a narrow informational bot-
tleneck. However, this process can also introduce representational
interference: token-level information that is not directly useful for
semantic matching, such as recurrent positional patterns, special-
token artifacts, or other non-semantic cues, may be absorbed into
the embedding representation and distort its true semantic con-
tent [6, 15, 25]. When this noise accumulates, it fundamentally
limits the discriminative power of the resulting embeddings in
downstream retrieval tasks.
sections.content: This issue becomes particularly important in light of the attention sink phenomenon, where certain positions attract disproportionately large attention despite carrying limited semantic content [25, 28]. Since the final retrieval representation is obtained by pooling or selecting from contextualized token representations, such artificial attention bias can cause non-semantic information to become deeply entangled with content-bearing tokens [8, 33], thereby diluting the overall sequence representation. Standard retrieval fine-tuning addresses this issue only indirectly: contrastive objectives improve querypassage alignment at the macro embedding level, but they do not explicitly control how residual tokenlevel information is represented or routed before pooling. Consequently, conventional retrieval optimization may still leave residual token-level information entangled with the embedding representation, leaving gap in how we optimize dense retrievers. In this work, we focus on how such residual information is handled during retrieval encoding by proposing simple yet highly effective architectural intervention. We use trainable [DUMP] tokens as input prefixes during embedding model training. These prefix tokens participate in contextualization before the sequence is compressed into single embedding, acting as dedicated semantic buffers. By absorbing attention associated with uninformative CIKM 26, November 0711, 2026, Rome, Italy Seongtae Hong, Youngjoon Jang, Jungseob Lee, Chanjun Park, and Heuiseok Lim signals, they help reduce the influence of residual token-level information that would otherwise be mixed into the embedding representation. Crucially, the method does not require modifying the core model architecture, introducing auxiliary losses, or changing the retrieval objective, making it highly scalable plug-and-play solution. Experiments on six diverse embedding models show that our method yields average relative improvements of 2.46% on standard retrieval benchmarks and 2.41% under long-context retrieval settings, demonstrating robust generalization. Further analyses show that the number of prefix tokens affects performance in nonmonotonic manner, while token-level inspection indicates that the added prefixes successfully change attention patterns associated with residual or uninformative tokens, effectively routing noise away from the final sequence representation.

sections.title:
2 RELATED WORK
Dense retrieval models encode queries and documents into fixed-
dimensional representations and compare them in a shared embed-
ding space to enable highly efficient semantic matching. In practice,
these models typically obtain sequence-level embeddings through
pooling or token-selection strategies, such as [CLS], mean, or last-
token pooling [2, 8, 14]. Although these strategies provide a simple
way to aggregate contextualized token representations, they also
create a severe compression bottleneck, as heterogeneous token-
level information is collapsed into a single retrieval vector, often
causing fine-grained semantic details to be lost. Prior work has
recognized this bottleneck in dense passage retrieval and proposed
specialized pre-training strategies to improve the quality of the
compressed representation [16, 26]. However, while these methods
enhance the general representation space, they do not inherently re-
solve the internal routing of noisy or uninformative signals during
the actual encoding phase.
sections.content: Recent studies on Transformer attention dynamics further suggest that not all token-level information contributes equally to the final semantic representation. In particular, the attention sink phenomenon shows that certain tokens can attract disproportionately large attention scores despite carrying limited semantic content [10, 20, 25, 28]. Driven by the softmax operation that forces attention allocation [18, 34], such behavior can help stabilize autoregressive generation, but it inadvertently introduces representational interference in embedding models, where the pooled vector is strictly expected to reflect the pure semantic content of the input. Related observations have also been made in vision Transformers, where learnable register tokens are introduced to absorb high-norm outlier information and reduce non-semantic artifacts in feature maps [6]. These studies directly motivate our use of trainable [DUMP] prefix tokens to provide dedicated structural pathway that absorbs residual or non-semantic information during retrieval encoding, yielding cleaner and more discriminative sequence representations.

sections.title:
3 Methods
We use [DUMP] tokens as trainable prefixes during embedding
model training, aiming to reduce residual token-level information
by providing dedicated slots for the model to route non-semantic
attention. The model architecture and retrieval objective remain
sections.content: unchanged. We first describe the encoding process and then present the retrieval training objective.

3.1 Dump-Token Conditioned Encoding
We describe the encoding process of an embedding model and then
explain how [DUMP] tokens are incorporated as input prefixes. Let
𝑞 and 𝑝 denote a query and a passage, respectively. For an input
text 𝑥 ∈ {𝑞, 𝑝}, a standard embedding model maps 𝑥 into a fixed-
dimensional representation through tokenization, model encoding,
and pooling. We add special tokens, denoted as [DUMP], to the
tokenizer vocabulary. In practice, we use 𝐾 indexed [DUMP] tokens,
i.e., [DUMP1], . . . , [DUMP𝐾 ]. The embeddings of these tokens are
initialized in the model’s embedding matrix and updated jointly
with the model parameters during retrieval fine-tuning. For 𝑥 ∈
{𝑞, 𝑝}, we prepend [DUMP] tokens:

During the forward pass, these prefix tokens interact with the regular text tokens via self-attention, allowing them to absorb structural or uninformative noise. The resulting embedding is computed as: (cid:101)𝐸𝜃 (𝑥) = pooling (𝑀𝜃 (𝑇 ( 𝑥))) , (2) where 𝑇 () denotes the tokenizer, 𝑀𝜃 denotes the embedding model, and pooling() denotes the pooling strategy. Crucially, the pooling strategy still operates on its default target (e.g., the [CLS] or last token), while the contextualized representation is influenced by interactions with the [DUMP] prefixes, which are introduced to reduce representational interference. The same prefixed encoding is used during both fine-tuning and inference. The [DUMP] tokens receive no separate supervision or auxiliary objective, and their embeddings are updated only through the retrieval loss.

Overall, our method consistently improves the average performance across all evaluated models, indicating that adding trainable prefix tokens is broadly effective for retrieval embedding learning. The gains are consistent across both encoder and decoder architectures; for example, ettin-decoder improves from 0.4377 to 0.4775 on average, while EuroBERT improves from 0.5786 to 0.5884. These consistent improvements support our hypothesis that assigning dedicated [DUMP] positions acts as useful auxiliary buffer to reduce representational interference during querypassage encoding. Since the model architecture and retrieval objective remain unchanged, these results demonstrate that trainable prefix tokens provide simple yet effective way to improve retrieval representations without requiring auxiliary losses or structural modifications. Long-Context Retrieval Results. Table 2 presents the LongEmbed evaluation results, where inputs are substantially longer than in standard retrieval benchmarks. This setting poses stronger compression challenge because the final pooled embedding must encode information from larger number of contextualized token representations. Our method consistently improves over the base models; for example, gte-en-mlm improves from 0.4797 to 0.5024, and ettin-decoder improves from 0.3330 to 0.3498. These gains suggest that trainable prefix tokens remain effective under longcontext encoding, where residual token-level information can have larger influence on the final pooled representation. sections.title: 5.2 The Role of Dump Tokens
sections.content: Setup. To understand how [DUMP] tokens affect internal representations, we analyze token-level representations and attention routing using gte-en-mlm-base on LongEmbed NQ. In the [DUMP] setting, the model is trained with four prepended [DUMP] tokens, denoted as D1D4. We group tokens into the sequence representation token ([CLS]), the learned prefix tokens (D1D4), and lowinformation tokens, identified using NLTK English stopwords. Motivated by prior work showing that Transformer artifacts can be associated with unusually high-norm token representations [6], Figure 2: Token-level analysis of the [DUMP] mechanism using gte-en-mlm-base. Panel (a) compares token-group activation scales measured by the mean L2 norm. Panel (b) visualizes the attention distribution from low-information tokens to [CLS] and D1D4, with D1D4 ordered by prefix position. Panel (a) measures the mean L2 norm of final-layer hidden states to compare activation scales across token groups. Panel (b) measures last-layer self-attention from low-information tokens to [CLS] and D1D4, averaged over attention heads, and reports the weights after 105 scaling for readability. Results. Figure 2 summarizes the token-level analysis. As shown in Panel (a), the baseline model exhibits relatively high activation norms for low-information tokens, suggesting that these tokens can carry disproportionately large internal activations. With [DUMP] tokens, the L2 norm of low-information tokens is reduced, while the learned prefixes (D1D4) form stable activation range close to the [CLS] token. Panel (b) further shows that attention from low-information tokens is redistributed away from [CLS] and toward the learned prefixes. These results suggest that [DUMP] tokens provide alternative prefix positions to which attention from Reducing Representational Interference in Retrieval Embeddings with Trainable Prefix Tokens CIKM 26, November 0711, 2026, Rome, Italy low-information tokens is redirected, thereby reducing their direct influence on the sequence representation.

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
We investigated whether trainable [DUMP] tokens can reduce rep-
resentational interference in embedding models when prepended
to the input text. Our approach preserves the original model archi-
tecture, pooling function, and retrieval objective, while allowing
the added prefix tokens to be learned through the same contrastive
training process. Across retrieval and long-context benchmarks, our
method consistently improves over finetuned baselines, showing
that learnable input prefixes can enhance retrieval representations
without additional supervision or architectural changes. Beyond
overall retrieval gains, our analysis indicates that [DUMP] tokens
can change how low-information token signals are represented and
attended to during encoding, providing evidence that the improve-
ment is linked to internal representation behavior rather than only
external performance differences. Overall, these findings suggest
that trainable prefix tokens offer a simple and effective way to im-
prove retrieval embeddings while preserving the underlying model
architecture.
